transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brings you in today?

Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. Well, I guess what finally made me come in is... well, it’s mostly work-related, or at least that’s where I’m noticing it the most right now. I work as a receptionist and information clerk, which means I’m always juggling a lot of little details, and normally I'm great at it, I really am. I have my associate's degree, I'm organized, I know how to handle the front desk. 

But lately, I’ve started just... losing my place. I'll be right in the middle of scheduling appointments on the computer—and our system is so finicky, if you don't pay attention it messes up the whole daily log for everyone else—and I'll just completely blank on what I was doing. Or I'll be out front working on the lobby displays, organizing the brochures and making sure the information packets look presentable for the visitors, and my mind just completely slips off track. 

It's like I can't stay focused on the one thing I'm actually trying to do because I’m so busy thinking about what I might have overlooked. I'll be standing there holding a stack of flyers, and my brain is just miles away, wondering if I forgot to pass on a message to one of the managers or if I missed a step in the morning opening routine. It’s just making it really hard to concentrate on my actual job, and I just can't seem to snap myself back into the present moment when it happens.
Have you been feeling down, sad, or hopeless most of the time lately, even outside of work?

No, no, I wouldn't say I've been feeling sad. It's not like a dark cloud or anything like that, and I don't feel hopeless. I have a good life, you know? My husband is wonderful, my kids are doing well, and like I said, I usually really like my job. I've been at the front desk for almost six years now, and I know everyone, and they know me. So it's not a sadness thing. I don't cry for no reason or feel like getting out of bed is impossible. I get up just fine, I make my coffee, I get dressed—I always make sure I look professional because I'm the first face people see when they walk in the door. It's just that my brain won't turn off. It's not sadness, it's just this constant spinning. I'll be driving to work, and the radio is on, but I'm not even hearing the music because I'm already mentally going through the mail sorting process and worrying if the courier is going to be late again like he was last Tuesday, which threw off my whole afternoon. So, no, definitely not depressed or hopeless. Just... distracted, I guess? And worried about making a mistake because I can't keep my thoughts straight.
Do you find that you worry much more than you used to, or that you can't control your worrying thoughts even when you try?

Oh, absolutely. Yes, I worry so much more than I used to, and it’s exactly like you said—I just can't seem to control it. It’s like my brain has a mind of its own, if that makes sense. I mean, I’ve always been a little bit of a planner, you know, making sure the kids’ schedules are set and the front desk is running smoothly, but this is different. Now, it’s just this constant stream of “what ifs.” 

And the worst part is, I try to stop it. I really do. I’ll catch myself worrying about something silly, like whether I locked the supply cabinet or if I sent that email to maintenance about the squeaky chair in the lobby. And I’ll literally say to myself, out loud sometimes if no one is around, "Sunny, it's handled. You checked it twice." But it doesn't work. The thought just keeps looping around in my head, like a record skipping. 

And then, because I can't let that one thing go, it sort of snowballs. Like, if I'm worrying about the supply cabinet, then suddenly I'm worrying about whether we have enough printer toner for the week, and if I didn't order the toner, then the billing department can't print their invoices, and then the whole office is going to be mad at me. It just goes from one concern to another, and pretty soon I'm just standing there, checking all these little details in my head over and over again, trying to make sure I haven't ruined everything. It’s exhausting, honestly. I never used to be like this. I used to be able to just leave work at work, but now I’m practically doing inventory in my head while I’m trying to make dinner for my family.
Have you noticed any physical changes when you're worrying, like feeling restless, tired, or having tense muscles?

Well, yes, actually, now that you mention it. It’s funny you bring up muscles because I was just telling my husband the other day—he was rubbing my shoulders while we were watching TV, well, he was watching TV, I was just sort of sitting there staring at the screen but really thinking about whether I’d remembered to forward the main phone line to the answering service before I locked up—and he said, "Sunny, you feel like a rock." And he’s right. I didn't even realize it until he touched my shoulders, but they were just completely knotted up. 

It’s like I carry all that worrying right here in my neck and shoulders. Especially at work. I mean, at the front desk, I have to keep up appearances, right? I’m the receptionist, so I’m the first point of contact. When people walk in, whether it’s a delivery driver or a new client or just one of the managers coming back from lunch, I have to be the one to look up, smile, say hello, and ask how I can help them. And I do! I still smile, I still greet everyone, I still help them find where they need to go or answer their questions. But inside? Inside, I just feel so... wound tight. 

It’s like my shoulders are creeping up around my ears the whole time I’m sitting there. I’ll be typing an email or sorting the incoming mail into those little slots we have behind the desk—which, by the way, are terribly designed because the slots are too narrow for the larger envelopes, so I always have to fold them or leave them in a separate pile, which just adds to the clutter and makes me worry I’m going to lose something important—and while I’m doing all that, I just feel this incredible tension. It’s like I’m just sitting there, physically braced, waiting for something to go wrong. Like I’m waiting for the phone to ring with someone yelling at me because I messed up a schedule, or waiting for a manager to come out and tell me I forgot a crucial step in the morning routine. I don't really feel tired, per se, but I definitely feel that restlessness and that tightness. It's just this constant, physical feeling of being on edge, even when I'm smiling at someone across the counter.

Have you ever had sudden episodes where your heart races, you feel short of breath, or you feel like something terrible is about to happen—even if you weren't thinking about something specific at the time?

No, I don't think so. Not out of nowhere like that. I mean, my heart definitely beats faster when I'm in the middle of a really stressful moment—like when all three phone lines are ringing at once, and the FedEx guy is standing there tapping his foot waiting for a signature, and someone from accounting is asking me where the mail is even though I haven't had a second to sort it yet. When that happens, sure, I feel a little flustered, maybe my chest gets a little tight just because I'm trying to do ten things at once and I'm worried I'm going to drop the ball. But it's always because of something that's actually happening, you know? 

It's never just... out of the blue. I've never been just sitting on the couch or driving in the car and suddenly felt like I couldn't breathe or like the world was ending for no reason. It's always tied to my worry. If I'm feeling overwhelmed, it's because my brain is going through that whole list of things I might have forgotten to do at the desk, or I'm stressing over whether I put the right postage on that certified letter yesterday. It's the thoughts that get me worked up, not just my body reacting on its own. So, no, I wouldn't say I've ever had an episode like what you're describing, where it just hits me without a specific trigger. It's just this constant, humming anxiety about all the details I have to keep track of, not a sudden attack of anything.
